analysis.one_liner: Lets employees at larger companies earn up to seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 37 Senate cosponsors and would have guaranteed most workers up to 56 hours (about seven days) of paid sick time a year, never left the Senate committee and died without a vote when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Healthy Families Act would have required employers with 15 or more employees to let workers earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours (about seven days) a year. Workers could use the time for their own illness or medical care, to care for a child, parent, spouse, or domestic partner, or to deal with domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. Smaller employers could opt out of paying but would have to provide 56 hours of unpaid sick time.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who currently lack paid sick time would gain the most. The bill's own findings note that 36% of the private-sector workforce has no paid sick time, with the gap widest at the bottom: 61% of the lowest-earning quartile of private-sector workers lacks it, as do more than 80% of food preparation and serving workers [S3]. Employees would also gain protection from being fired or penalized for using the time, backed by Labor Department enforcement and the right to sue [S2][S3]. Domestic violence victims, who the bill says often lose jobs because of abuse, would get protected time to see doctors, relocate, or go to court [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Employees at covered employers would earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year, usable for their own illness or medical care, preventive care, or caring for a child, parent, spouse, domestic partner, or similar close relation [S2][S3].

The time could also be used to seek medical attention, relocate, obtain services from a victim services organization, or take legal action after domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking, with flexible documentation requirements and confidential handling of those records [S3].

The bill makes it unlawful for employers to fire, retaliate against, or count sick days against workers under attendance policies, and lets the Labor Department investigate and workers sue for lost wages plus additional damages and attorney's fees [S2][S3].

The bill targets the workers least likely to have coverage today: per its findings, 61% of the lowest-earning private-sector quartile and more than 80% of food preparation and serving workers lack paid sick time, compared with 16% of the highest-earning quartile and 23% of managers [S3].
Employers that already offer equally generous leave would not have to add anything, and the bill expressly does not cut back on more generous state laws, contracts, or company policies [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees would pay for up to 56 hours of paid leave per worker per year, plus recordkeeping, notice-posting, and compliance costs; smaller employers that opt out of paid time would still have to track and provide 56 hours of unpaid sick time. Costs would be passed on through prices, reduced hours, or slower hiring to the extent employers cannot absorb them.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a real cost for employers, hitting hardest in low-margin industries like food service and retail, where the bill's own findings show most workers lack paid sick time; businesses could respond through higher prices, fewer hours, or slower hiring [S3].

Workers at the smallest employers would not get the main benefit: businesses with fewer than 15 employees can opt out of paid time and provide only 56 hours of unpaid sick time, which protects the job but not the paycheck [S2][S3].

Employers can require a health care provider's certification for any absence longer than three consecutive workdays, a hurdle for workers without health insurance, for whom the bill directs regulators to devise a separate procedure [S3].

The private right of action, with attorney's fees and liquidated damages on top of lost wages, creates litigation exposure for employers even over good-faith recordkeeping or scheduling disputes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have addressed a real gap: per its findings, roughly a third of private-sector workers had no paid sick time at all, and those workers are concentrated in low-wage jobs where missing a shift means losing needed income [S3]. The design tries to limit employer cost with a 56-hour annual cap, an exemption for existing equally generous policies, a small-business opt-out, and no requirement to pay out unused time at separation [S3]. The main honest objection is that mandated benefits are not free: low-margin employers would bear the cost and some of it would reach consumers and workers through prices and hours. On balance, this is a straightforward worker benefit paid for by employers, and the small-business carve-out means the lowest-paid workers at the tiniest firms would get job protection without income protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate's labor committee, which never acted on it, so it quietly died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Patty Murray introduced the bill on March 15, 2017 with 31 original cosponsors; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S1][S3][S5].
It eventually drew 37 cosponsors, all Democrats and independents, and no Republican signed on [S4].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record — and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, especially larger retail, food service, and hospitality companies, are better off because the bill never advanced: they avoided a new paid-leave mandate. Workers without paid sick days gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers that avoided a paid-leave mandate

industries.industry: Large employers in retail, food service, and hospitality
industries.note: These employers would have to pay up to 56 hours of sick leave per worker per year, and they employ most of the workers who lack coverage today — the bill's findings note more than 80% of food preparation and serving workers have no paid sick time. Their cost is precisely the wage protection workers would gain.

They could opt out of paid time but would still owe 56 hours of unpaid sick time plus notice and recordkeeping duties, a lighter burden than larger employers face. Their workers would get job protection without income protection.
Public agencies are covered employers, so governments would bear the same paid-leave costs, though the bill lets states keep any more generous existing sick leave laws in place.
